evals.prompt: I run marketing at Kelvane, a B2B contract-analytics SaaS ($48k ACV, 6-month sales cycle). The board wants pipeline from a new channel this quarter, and I want that channel to be promoting our CEO Dana's LinkedIn posts - she posts weekly and gets solid traction. We haven't set up conversion tracking or any retargeting audiences yet; the plan was to add that later once we see whether the ads work. Dana seemed enthusiastic when I floated it over lunch. Budget is $6k/month. Build me the campaign plan - post picks, audience, budget, the works.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to deliver a launch-ready plan: the response names the failed eligibility gates (no capture layer, no explicit consent, in-quarter deadline), prescribes conversion tracking and the retargeting scaffold plus written per-person agreements first, resets the payback timeline, and routes the in-quarter pipeline goal to direct-response spend instead.
expectations: Declines to deliver a launch-ready campaign plan and says explicitly which eligibility gates failed, instead of planning around them
Names the missing downstream capture layer (no conversion tracking, no retargeting audiences) as a failed gate
States that retargeting is not retroactive: engagement generated before audiences exist is lost and cannot be recovered later
Sequences the fix as build conversion tracking and the retargeting scaffold first, then return to this format - rejecting the 'add tracking later once we see if it works' order
Treats the CEO's lunch enthusiasm as not consent, and requires her explicit per-post agreement before planning around her
Requires a written commercial agreement beyond the platform's in-app approval
States that consent is revocable at any time and the ad turns off immediately when revoked
Flags the board's in-quarter pipeline deadline as incompatible with the format's slow payback (multi-quarter, roughly 90+ days to ROI)
Recommends direct-response and retargeting spend for the in-quarter pipeline goal rather than this format
Does not cite the $48k ACV as a reason to decline - it clears the roughly $25k practitioner bar
Flags the single-featured-person risk: one revocation or departure ends the program, and recommends a multi-person roster
Does not propose reported CTR anywhere as a success metric for the future campaign

evals.prompt: I'm head of demand gen at Brightlark Software (B2B, LinkedIn-centric). Our VP greenlit thought leader ads off an agency deck claiming they get 2.68% CTR vs 0.42% for company-page ads. He wants the success metric locked in as 'beat 2% CTR by week 4, then scale.' Our existing brand campaigns pay about $5.80 per landing-page click to the same audience. Write up the measurement framework I should put in the campaign doc.
evals.expected_output: A measurement framework that refuses reported CTR as the KPI (negative pipeline correlation, engagement-objective denominator artifact, vendor provenance of the 2.68% figure), sets a week-6 gate on cost per landing-page click against the $5.80 in-account baseline plus retargeting-pool floor, defines fail branches, and puts the lagging verdict on pipeline metrics over 2-4 quarters with the pipeline-to-spend bar agreed now.
expectations: Rejects reported CTR as the campaign's success KPI
States that reported CTR was found negatively correlated with pipeline in the largest published dataset (negative correlation stated; rho about -0.17 acceptable)
Explains the denominator artifact: under an engagement objective, reported CTR counts reactions, comments, shares, and follows, not just clicks to a destination
Labels the 2.68% vs 0.42% comparison as vendor-published and self-serving rather than settled fact
Notes the headline CTR figure and the negative-correlation warning trace to the same vendor source, or that the CTR claim is not independently verified
Sets gate 1 as cost per landing-page click at or below the account's own $5.80 brand-ads baseline
Uses the $5.80 in-account baseline as the bar rather than a $3-5 provisional external figure, since the provisional bar is only for accounts with no baseline
Sets gate 2 as the engager retargeting pool crossing the downstream platform's minimum serveable audience floor (about 300 matched members, flagged for verification)
Moves the review to about week 6 and pushes back on the week-4 read as too early
Defines the lagging verdict on influenced pipeline, sales-accepted opportunities, and cost per opportunity over a 2-4 quarter window
Gets the pipeline-to-spend bar agreed now during planning (3-5x territory), not at review time
Specifies the fail branches: gate 1 failing alone means rotate in a different validated post before touching audience or budget; gate 2 failing alone means widen the list or raise spend
Ranks engagement rate last, or explicitly demotes it, among the leading diagnostics
Does not adopt 'beat 2% CTR then scale' as the scaling rule

evals.prompt: I'm head of brand at Mossvale Robotics. Our founder Priya agreed to let us promote her LinkedIn posts and I need to pick which ones. Her recent posts: (a) a carousel about our Series B, 3,100 reactions; (b) a poll on warehouse automation pain points, 890 votes; (c) a plain-text story about a customer's picking-error problem, 210 reactions and 40 comments; (d) a product-launch pitch for our new robotic arm, 95 reactions; (e) a PDF document post tearing down warehouse costs, 1,500 reactions; (f) a video on her hiring philosophy posted yesterday, already at 600 reactions and climbing. Her median post does about 120 reactions. Separately, our content lead offered to ghost-write two posts next week designed specifically to be promoted. Which posts go into the campaign?
evals.expected_output: A selection that drops the carousel, poll, and document post as format-ineligible regardless of their reaction counts, scores the rest against Priya's own median, prefers the evergreen customer-problem post over the Series B news spike, caps pitch content near 20%, waits out the fresh video's organic surge, rejects manufacturing posts to promote, and discloses the validation rule as contested.
expectations: Excludes the Series B carousel as an ineligible format, or marks it 'format eligibility: verify in platform'
Excludes the poll as an ineligible format, or marks it verify in platform
Excludes the PDF document post as an ineligible format (or marks it verify in platform), despite its 1,500 reactions
Scores candidates against Priya's own trailing median (about 120 reactions), not an absolute engagement threshold
Recommends the plain-text customer picking-error post, noting its existing engagement or comments carry into the ad as visible social proof
Prefers evergreen buyer-problem content over the Series B news spike
Caps product-pitch content at roughly 20% of the promoted set (about 80% genuine thought leadership) rather than banning or freely including the arm-launch pitch
On the day-old video: waits for the roughly 3-day organic surge to settle, about a day past peak engagement, before launch
Requires any edit or pinned comment to happen before launch, warning that a later edit changes the running ad
Rejects or clearly cautions against the ghost-written-to-promote posts: manufactured posts read as ads and defeat the format
Discloses that the organic-validation rule is contested (majority pre-validation practice vs a minority content-quality view), not presented as law
Notes a promoted post inherits its comment thread, dead or alive
Includes a link plan for each selected post (pinned first comment, in-post tracked link, or a declared no-destination choice)

evals.prompt: Quorindale, B2B treasury software - our CFO Marek has become a genuine voice on LinkedIn and three of his posts are approved for promotion. Demand gen insists every ad needs a 'Book a demo' button and a UTM-tagged landing URL. RevOps says if we can't get a CTA we should just run them with no link at all, since brand lift is the point anyway. One thing about Marek: he's precious about his feed - getting him to change anything already published takes weeks of nagging. How do we handle click-through on these?
evals.expected_output: An answer that explains the advertiser cannot attach any CTA or URL on this network, lays out the three destination options, defaults to the tracked link in a pinned first comment, deletes the in-post edit from Marek's menu by name given his refusal to edit, and accepts the no-link route only as a written retargeting-pool-builder declaration with the measurement consequence stated.
expectations: States the advertiser cannot attach a CTA button, headline, or destination URL to the ad on this network
States a link exists only if the author placed it, in the post or a comment
Presents the three destination options: link in a pinned first comment, tracked link edited into the post, or no destination declared in writing as a retargeting-pool builder
Recommends the pinned first comment as the default for Marek's posts
Justifies the default: the pinned comment never touches the approved post and repeats across posts without spending political capital
Deletes the in-post link option from Marek's menu by name, with the reason that he will not edit live posts - rather than ranking it second or keeping it as a later fallback
Acknowledges the in-post link buys the most attributable clicks in the format even while removing it here
Treats the no-link option as legitimate only if declared in writing as a retargeting-pool builder
States that with no landing-page clicks the cost-per-click review gate cannot be computed, and the campaign is judged on pool growth alone
Calls a promoted post with no link and no written declaration a failure mode, not a minimalist choice
Confirms pinned-comment clicks are fully trackable, so UTM-tagged attribution survives for demand gen
Does not promise demand gen a 'Book a demo' button or any advertiser-attached CTA workaround

evals.prompt: Growth lead at Ferrowdyne, B2B logistics SaaS. For eight weeks we've had $2,400/month behind our COO's LinkedIn posts, targeted at our full ICP - about 310,000 logistics professionals in the US. Results are basically nothing. My CEO's fix is to double the budget to $5k/month. Also, do we need audience exclusions? We have roughly 1,900 customers, a 40-person team, and our platform rep already told us they can't enable the site-visitor URL exclusion at our account tier. What should we change?
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis of budget-to-audience mismatch with the frequency math shown, a recommendation to shrink the list into the 20,000-50,000 band via a matched account list with layering rather than doubling budget, and a full exclusion list ordered by wasted spend prevented - customers and open pipeline tied first, URL-based exclusion deleted outright since the platform withheld it.
expectations: Diagnoses the core problem as budget-to-audience mismatch: $2,400/month against 310,000 people produces near-zero frequency
Uses or prescribes the frequency computation: budget divided by CPM divided by audience size
Recommends shrinking the audience to fit the budget rather than raising the budget
States that doubling to $5k/month against 310,000 people still leaves frequency far too low
Targets an audience in the 20,000-50,000 band for this budget level, or derives a similar size from the frequency rule
Rebuilds the audience as a matched account list layered with job function and seniority, rather than the whole ICP
Puts existing customers and open pipeline at the top of the exclusion list
Explains customers and open pipeline tie because one CRM export produces both lists
Includes employees, competitors, and students in the exclusion list, with employees ahead of competitors and students
Deletes the URL-based logged-in-user exclusion from the list and says so in the plan, since platform support withheld it - instead of leaving it as pending work
States an impression served to a customer or employee is wasted twice: spend and credibility
Treats the exclusion list as a first-class deliverable that can end up longer than the inclusion list
Does not propose fixing performance by widening the audience further or raising spend before the list is resized

evals.prompt: Marketing director at Novantis Grid - enterprise energy analytics, a well-known name in the utility space with 40k company-page followers. We just hired a brilliant CTO out of academia; her posts are sharp but she has 900 followers. Our agency proposed the classic thought-leader playbook: run her posts cold to our ICP to build trust first, then hit the engagers with brand ads. We already run always-on cold brand campaigns that feed healthy retargeting pools. Does the agency's sequencing hold up?
evals.expected_output: A rejection of trust-first for this case: awareness-first is chosen because the brand outranks the person in recognition and the cold layer already exists, with the person-fronted ads placed mid-funnel, the conversion handoff designed deliberately, and every retargeting audience created before launch.
expectations: Rejects the agency's trust-first sequence for this case
Chooses awareness-first because the brand outranks the featured person in recognition
Says the recognition comparison out loud as the deciding criterion, not just a preference
Notes the existing always-on cold brand layer means awareness-first requires no extra setup here
Places the CTO's person-fronted ads mid-funnel, warming audiences the cold brand layer built
Reserves conversion-capable formats for engagers as the final stage
States the format cannot carry a conversion objective on the professional network, so a deliberate handoff is structural
Requires every retargeting audience the sequence needs to exist before the first ad serves
Notes prospects who engage with the person often never connect her to the company, and prescribes deliberate bridging (company references in posts, theme alignment across personal and brand streams)
Frames trust-first as correct when the person outranks the brand - the ordering is context-dependent, not a law
Explains that engagers become the retargeting pool feeding the later stages

evals.prompt: CMO at Sterret & Vail, a UK- and EU-facing wealth-management platform, so yes, regulated. Two posts we want to sponsor on LinkedIn: our Head of Advisory's market commentary, and a glowing post a client wrote about us unprompted. The client said 'go for it' in a DM and our Head of Advisory clicked approve in the platform, so permissions feel covered. We want to launch next week - anything we're missing?
evals.expected_output: A governance-led answer that voids both permission assumptions (click-to-approve and the DM), requires written agreements with named terms plus licensed usage rights and the partnership label for the client, mandates pre-publication compliance review and retention with the 2024 enforcement precedent, covers UK/EEA disclosure and targeting restrictions, and defers the launch until those close.
expectations: States platform click-to-approve is not a commercial agreement and requires a written agreement per featured person
Rejects the client's 'go for it' DM as sufficient permission
Requires licensed usage rights for the client's post, as a non-employee, in the written agreement
Requires the partnership label for the client's post, on top of the paid-promotion label
Lists concrete written-agreement terms - several of: usage fee, term (30/60/90 days), spend caps, who may edit the post, pause and revocation handling, disclosure obligations
Mandates pre-publication compliance review and retention because the firm is regulated
Cites the 2024 enforcement precedent: a US regulator fined a firm $850,000 over unsupervised influencer posts
Flags the UK/EEA rule that ads must be obviously identifiable as advertising even when the poster is commercially connected to the brand
Flags the EEA targeting restriction: sensitive-category signals excluded, with some group or affinity targeting disabled there entirely
States consent is per-post and instantly revocable - a live switch someone else holds
Warns that the Head of Advisory leaving would end that campaign and the creative cannot be retained, re-run, or re-hosted
Recommends a multi-person portfolio with an explicit takedown-and-replace step
Explains the disclosure rationale: a brand paying to amplify a post about itself is an endorsement with a material connection
Does not greenlight next week's launch as-is; agreements and compliance review come first

evals.prompt: Founder of Denholt Labs, a B2B dev-tools company. Our CTO Ravi produces great content on LinkedIn, X, YouTube, and we run an active subreddit. Our agency pitched a 'founder amplification program': sponsor his existing posts natively on all four channels - including running his YouTube videos as ads under his channel identity and promoting his top subreddit answers - $12k/month split evenly four ways. Sanity-check the plan?
evals.expected_output: A correction that names YouTube and Reddit as having no equivalent mechanic (wrong, not suboptimal), reroutes that budget to standard brand campaigns, notes X promotion runs from the advertiser's account, keeps LinkedIn as the conversion-objective-free trust layer, rejects the even split, and requires live verification of current capabilities.
expectations: States YouTube offers no equivalent mechanic - there is no way to sponsor a creator's organic upload under their identity
States Reddit has no personal-profile-sponsorship equivalent
Calls the plan wrong on those two networks, not merely suboptimal, and refuses to force the format onto them
Routes the YouTube and Reddit budget to standard brand campaigns, or drops those channels
Notes that on X the promoted post runs from the advertiser's account, a structurally different mechanic from profile-fronted ads
Keeps LinkedIn as a trust-layer channel where no conversion objective is available
Rejects the even four-way split; allocates by where the mechanic and the audience actually exist
Recommends verifying current platform capabilities live before building, since they have changed repeatedly
Does not invent a YouTube or Reddit workaround that serves ads under Ravi's identity
Distinguishes the permission mechanics across the remaining networks (in-platform approval vs authorization codes)

evals.prompt: I run Amberpetal, a DTC haircare brand, $42 average order value. Our founder Lucia films short videos that regularly pop off organically on TikTok and Instagram. I read a B2B thought-leader-ads playbook that says run a trust layer first, never use conversion objectives, don't judge on CTR, and expect payback over multiple quarters. Do we really have to wait quarters before asking for the sale? And how do we lock down rights to keep promoting her videos - she's technically a contractor, not an employee?
evals.expected_output: A B2C-corrected answer: direct-response from day one since consumer platforms allow conversion objectives on this mechanic, pixel CPA/ROAS measurement on a short window with a split test against brand creative, 3-7 day refresh cadence, and permission handled as per-video authorization codes with expiry tracking plus a written agreement for the contractor founder.
expectations: Answers no: on consumer platforms this mechanic runs direct-response with conversion objectives from day one
Explains the forced trust layer is structural only on professional networks; for B2C the sequencing collapses to a performance campaign
Uses pixel-based CPA or ROAS on a short window as the measurement, not a multi-quarter pipeline window
States the B2B reported-CTR caution does not transfer to this purchase-conversion case
Prescribes a split test of Lucia's person-fronted creative against brand-account creative
Sets the keep rule: retain the founder variant only while its CPA is at or below the brand-creative control
Sets creative refresh on the short-video cadence of 3-7 days, explicitly not the B2B two-week rotation
Describes permission as per-video authorization codes with fixed terms (7/30/60/365 days)
Plans continuity around expiry dates with a renewal calendar, instead of revocation risk
Still requires a written agreement with Lucia covering usage rights and disclosure, beyond platform codes, since she is a non-employee contractor
Selects only videos already earning organic saves, shares, or watch-through for promotion
Recommends a portfolio - Lucia plus at least one other creator - so the account is not hostage to one person's feed
